ethanol-95.classifiedAs: Hazards of denatured ethyl alcohol, which is mostly ethanol with other alcohols added, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H225: Highly flammable liquid and vapor
H315+H319: Causes skin and serious eye irritation

note.value:
The unknown liquid may be this: ethanol of 95% by mass in water, 20 to 45 mL in an open cylinder. The supplier's sheet is for its denatured ethyl alcohol, which has other alcohols added and is poisonous for them; the statements above are that sheet's. It keeps the liquid from heat, sparks, flames, oxidizers and acids, has it used where the air is changed, and calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: NOAA's record of ethanol says that the vapour is heavier than air and that a flame can run back along it; that clothing wet with it is taken off at once, since it can catch fire; and, for the eyes, flushing with water for 20 to 30 minutes and a hospital after.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

nacl-20.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid sodium chloride, the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H303: May be harmful if swallowed

note.value:
The unknown liquid may be this: sodium chloride of 20% by mass in water, 20 to 45 mL of it in an open cylinder. The same supplier's sheet for the solution, whose table of composition has this strength at its top, prints no signal word and no hazard statement: it classes its solution as not hazardous, and says that it is a laboratory chemical all the same, not for eating or drinking. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: the two other suppliers' sheets read, both for the solid, class it as not hazardous and ask only for more after a splash: 15 minutes or more of rinsing for the eyes, and a doctor seen at once.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

aluminium-pieces.classifiedAs: Hazards of aluminium metal, the solid and not its powder or dust, from a supplier's safety data sheet

note.value:
The unknown metal may be this: dry pieces of aluminium, slid into cold water, not a powder. The supplier's sheet for aluminium prints no signal word and no hazard statement. It says that the dust burns, that powder and dust give off heat with water, and that acids set hydrogen free. It calls for eye and face protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: a second supplier's sheet for aluminium shot keeps the metal from strong alkalis too, and says that it is the molten metal that reacts with water. For the eyes it asks flushing with water for 15 minutes or more and a doctor at once. NOAA's record marks the powder as reacting with water and catching fire in air: the powder is another matter.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

zinc-pieces.classifiedAs: Hazards of zinc metal, as shot, sheet, foil or granules, from a supplier's safety data sheet

note.value:
The unknown metal may be this: dry pieces of zinc, slid into cold water, not dust. The supplier's sheet for zinc as shot, sheet and foil prints no signal word and no hazard statement, puts the fire hazards with the dust, and keeps the metal from strong acids and bases. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: a second supplier's sheet for zinc shot says that hydrogen may come off zinc in water or damp air; here the pieces are in water only for the measurement. It names dermatitis, and for the eyes asks 15 minutes or more of flushing with water and a doctor at once. A third's calls zinc very toxic to water life: it is kept out of drains and waterways.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

copper-pieces.classifiedAs: Hazards of copper metal, the solid and not its powder or dust, from a supplier's safety data sheet

note.value:
The unknown metal may be this: dry pieces of copper, slid into cold water, not a powder. The supplier's sheet for copper prints no signal word and no hazard statement. It says that the metal in bulk does not burn, though its dust may, and keeps it from strong acids, nitric acid above all, and from strong oxidizers and halogens. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: NOAA's record of copper, from a federal guide to its dusts and mists, has skin that it touches washed promptly with soap and water, and the eyes washed at once with plenty of water, with medical attention immediately. It names sore eyes and nose and dermatitis as what the dust does: the dust is another matter.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.
